items.headline: OFAC designates 36 targets across Iran's civil aviation network under 'Operation Economic Outcast'
items.what_happened: On 8 September 2026, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated 36 targets under an action Treasury branded 'Operation Economic Outcast'. Twenty-seven are Iranian airlines, including Iran Air Tour, Iran Aseman Airlines, Kish Airlines, Qeshm Air and Saha Airlines, designated under Executive Order 13902 for operating in Iran's aviation sector. Of the nine remaining targets, eight entities and one individual, Ibrahim Ali Mohamed Mohamed Mahran, based across the UAE, Türkiye, Malaysia, Kazakhstan and the UK, were designated under Executive Order 13224, as amended, for roles including supporting Mahan Air, aircraft management, cargo services, logistics and general sales agent activity. Treasury cited different bases for different targets within that group, including material support, ownership or control, and leadership or official status, rather than a single uniform basis. Treasury separately suspended three general licences previously available under the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations. All property and interests in property of designated persons within US jurisdiction are blocked, and US persons are generally prohibited from transacting with them.
items.why_it_matters: This is a coordinated network designation, not a single-entity listing: OFAC paired direct designations of the Iranian airlines themselves with designations of third-country aviation-support businesses that keep those airlines operating, spread across five separate jurisdictions. For institutions with aviation, leasing, insurance or logistics exposure in the Gulf, Turkey or Central Asia, screening only against the airline names themselves misses the support layer this action specifically targets.
items.radar_implication: Re-screen aviation-adjacent counterparties, freight forwarders, aircraft lessors and cargo logistics providers in the UAE, Türkiye, Malaysia and Kazakhstan against the newly designated entities, not only against the Iranian airline names. One quarter of the targets, 9 of 36, were based outside Iran, illustrating how aviation-related sanctions exposure extends into third-country corporate and intermediary networks that a jurisdiction-based Iran filter alone would not catch. If your firm relied on any of the three now-suspended Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations general licences, confirm wind-down authority and any applicable deadline directly against OFAC's own suspension notice before processing further transactions.

items.headline: FinCEN links $17.5bn in suspicious activity to health care fraud, flags Puerto Rico Medicaid balance-manipulation pattern
items.what_happened: FinCEN published a Financial Trend Analysis, issued pursuant to Section 6206 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, analysing 5,702 Bank Secrecy Act reports filed by 471 financial institutions between 1 March 2025 and 28 February 2026 that identified approximately $17.5bn in suspicious activity linked to suspected health care fraud (completed and attempted transactions combined). Depository institutions filed 89% of the reports and accounted for 87% of the dollar volume. Home health care businesses were the most frequently identified type of suspected fraudulent provider, appearing in over a fifth of the dataset. FinCEN separately detailed a Puerto Rico-specific pattern in which Medicaid recipients allegedly withdrew funds shortly before an eligibility review to obtain a bank balance certification letter showing they qualified, then redeposited the funds within days; 59 Puerto Rican financial cooperatives filed 1,641 of the reports in the dataset, almost entirely describing this pattern.
items.why_it_matters: This is FinCEN's own aggregation of activity institutions are already filing, not a new typology firms are being asked to start looking for: the $17.5bn figure tells firms the scale of health care fraud-linked activity already sitting in SAR data industry-wide. The Puerto Rico balance-certification pattern is a mechanically specific scheme, funds pulled down before a review and restored days later, that a standard high-balance or high-turnover alert would likely miss, since neither the withdrawal nor the redeposit looks unusual in isolation.
items.radar_implication: If your transaction monitoring rules key off home health care, hospice, durable medical equipment or behavioural health provider codes, check whether a rule already exists for a short-window withdrawal-then-redeposit pattern timed against a customer-stated benefits review, rather than only generic high-cash-turnover thresholds. For institutions with Puerto Rico-based accounts, consider a dedicated look-back at cooperativa-filed SARs matching this pattern, since FinCEN's own data shows it concentrated overwhelmingly in that filer population. Confirm your SAR narrative templates for health care fraud already distinguish billing fraud (upcoding, phantom billing) from proceeds-placement typologies like this one, since the appropriate control response differs.

items.headline: NCA's National Economic Crime Centre ranks cryptoassets third among nine national economic-crime priorities in new annual report
items.source_name: National Crime Agency (National Economic Crime Centre)
items.what_happened: The NCA's National Economic Crime Centre (NECC) published its 2025-26 Annual Report, confirming cryptoassets as the third-ranked priority among the nine 'Economic Crime System Priorities' agreed with the FCA, HM Treasury and the Home Office as part of Economic Crime Plan 2 (the priorities themselves were published in July 2025; only professional enablers and politically exposed persons rank above cryptoassets). The report states the NECC is 'developing a more proactive and intelligence-led crypto capability' and cites 'the innovative use of crypto asset products to evade detection and move illicit value at scale' as a growing feature of the illicit finance landscape. It also updates figures for Operation Destabilise, the NECC's investigation into Russian-speaking cash-to-crypto laundering networks: 129 arrests and over £25m seized in cash and cryptoassets in the UK since 2022, plus a further $24m and over €2.6m seized internationally using intelligence the operation generated.
items.why_it_matters: This is a status confirmation of an existing priority ranking rather than a new designation, but the operational detail behind it, an intelligence-led crypto capability the NECC describes as still being built rather than already operating at scale, matters for how firms read NECC alerts and information requests in this space. The Destabilise figures also point to a shift in the laundering model: criminal cash is being converted to crypto specifically to move value across borders, not only to obscure it.
items.radar_implication: If your firm's crypto exposure risk rating still treats crypto as a peripheral or emerging risk category, this report is the NECC's own basis for treating it as a top-three national priority alongside professional enablers and PEPs, worth reflecting explicitly in your next risk assessment refresh. For firms handling cash-intensive businesses with subsequent crypto conversion, review whether your typologies cover a distinct 'cash-to-crypto swap' pattern rather than only conventional layering, since that is the specific mechanism the NECC attributes to the Destabilise network.

items.headline: NCA-wanted suspect arrested at Dublin Airport over alleged $23m fraud on Australian mining company
items.what_happened: Edwin Omokhuale, 39, was arrested by An Garda Síochána at Dublin Airport on 9 September 2026 as he attempted to board a flight to Paris, acting on an NCA warrant. The NCA states he is wanted in connection with money laundering linked to an alleged fraud of approximately $23m (around £17m) against an Australian mining company in early 2023, in which company employees were allegedly deceived into transferring funds to accounts controlled by UK-based fraudsters. Omokhuale, who lived in the UK at the time of the alleged fraud, appeared before a Dublin court on 10 September 2026 as extradition proceedings to the UK began. No charges have been determined by a UK court and the allegations remain unproven.
items.why_it_matters: The fraud allegedly ran through UK-based conduits, but the victim, an Australian mining company, and the point of arrest, Dublin, are both outside the UK, illustrating how a single fraud allegation can span three jurisdictions before an extradition even resolves who tries the case. For firms handling payments connected to mining or resources-sector counterparties, this is a reminder that business email compromise-style schemes are not confined to smaller corporates.
items.radar_implication: If your firm processes payments for mining, resources or extractives clients where instructions reference account changes or new counterparties, confirm your payment verification callback procedure requires an independently sourced phone number, not one supplied in the instruction itself, since that is the standard vector for this fraud pattern. Treat this as an open extradition matter in any adverse media screening: record it as wanted with unresolved allegations and extradition proceedings in progress, not as a conviction or a finalised fraud finding.
